text:
li: Ran a canary swap to fa-v3 kernels on the ng4g pool this morning. Observed ~8% throughput drop on the mid-sequence workload (seq ~256) vs fa-v2. p50 latency roughly same, p95/p99 nudged up. Posting quick notes and logs.

raj: which model and quant profile?

li: gpt-neox-20B, int8+qkv-swap profile we usually use. Workload: 70% seq<=64, 25% seq~256, 5% long tails ~1024. Batch target 64, continuous batching enabled.

emma: can you paste the perf numbers?

li: sure — raw numbers for the same 30m window, 8 concurrent workers per GPU.

```
kernel   | throughput tok/s | p50 ms | p95 ms | p99 ms
fa-v2    | 120k            | 18     | 65     | 130
fa-v3    | 110k            | 19     | 78     | 165
```

li: breakdown looks like fa-v3 wins on short seq single-request latency but regresses under mixed-batches.

darren: interesting — could be kernel selection heuristics picking the v3 path for midseq that can't pack workspace as efficiently. Any workspace allocation failures in logs?

li: saw a few "alloc_workspace_failed" and then fallback to slower matmul path. grep: ~0.7% of requests in window.

perf-bot: Canary: fa-v3 deployed to ng4g pool at 2026-03-19T09:03Z, monitoring window ended 2026-03-19T09:33Z. Regression alert triggered for throughput -7.9%.

raj: what about kv-cache behavior? midseq gets lots of partial prefix reuse which affects KV layout. fa-v3 changed KV packing from per-batch contiguous to per-request shard. That could increase fragmentation.

li: we instrumented KV occupancy: avg workspace utilization increased 12% with fa-v3, and fragmentation metric (free segments) also up. When fragmentation hits threshold, allocator falls back and triggers slower kernel.

emma: do we see correlation with request shape distribution per batch? maybe fa-v3 is sensitive to variance within a batch.

li: yes — synthetic repro: creating batches with 50% short(32) + 50% mid(256) shows similar drop. Uniform batches don't.

raj: hypothesis: kernel heuristics used sequence-len percentiles to pick tiling and workspace sizes. fa-v3's workspace estimator is tighter (less slack), so mixed batches occasionally oversubscribe and fall into slow path. Options: 1) widen estimator slack, 2) change batching to bucket by seq-length, 3) transiently prefer fa-v2 for mixed batches. Thoughts?

darren: (1) is fastest to try. add a 20% headroom and see if fallback rate drops. But headroom reduces theoretical throughput. (2) is bigger change but good long term: adapt batching to reduce intra-batch variance. (3) seems pragmatic: route by batch-variance.

li: trying (1) now. patch to runtime config:
```
kernel_selection:
  fa_v3:
    workspace_headroom: 1.2  # previously 1.0
```
Applying to canary in 5m.

perf-bot: canary config update applied to ng4g at 2026-03-19T09:45Z.

li: short update after 20m: fallback alloc rate down from 0.7% to 0.05%. Throughput recovered to within 1% of fa-v2 baseline for mixed workloads. p99 still slightly higher by ~10ms.

emma: nice. why p99 higher? maybe kernel path still not identical — fa-v3 uses different attention tiling which can elevate tail when one request in batch is long and stalls others. Also async scheduling interactions with our per-GPU worker thread pool.

raj: we should also test with bursty arrival — the estimator headroom can be adaptive: increase when mix variance goes up. Long-term, we probably want batching buckets + kernel hints.

darren: agree. action items:
- li: run a 4h canary with adaptive headroom and sample-bucketed batching enabled to compare. (li)
- emma: instrument per-request kernel path + worker blocking time to root cause p99s. (emma)
- raj: draft a small RFC for batch-shaping + kernel-fallback policy (prefer fa-v3 but auto-fall back to fa-v2 for high-variance batches). (raj)

li: logging snippet of fallback event for posterity:
```
[2026-03-19T09:11:23Z] req=0x7f3 alloc_workspace_failed fa_v3 -> fallback=matmul_slow path
metadata: seq_len=256 batch_ids=[4,7,9] batch_var=0.42 kv_segments_used=18/16
```

raj: that kv_segments_used > cap is the smoking gun. could we consider per-request compaction before kernel selection? cost vs benefit tradeoff.

emma: compaction might add CPU overhead and latency — maybe do it only when fragmentation crosses threshold.

darren: also consider metrics to detect degradation early and auto-roll config. We should add a tracer span to measure time spent in allocator -> kernel select -> kernel exec to isolate where the tail is.

li: agreed. I'll run the longer canary and post results. Thanks all :thumbsup:
